By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
An antibiotic so powerful that it should only be used as a last resort, is prescribed for minor infections, but the side effects are devastating and permanent.

Unique Selling Point:
Big Pharma usually wins. For 20 years patients have been ignored by their doctors, who disbelieve their symptoms, the European Medicines Agency has finally woken up. In 2018 the European Medicine Agency listened and recorded testimonies from patients and doctors across Europe of how this drug destroyed lives. So unique is that there are multiple international case studies whose testimonies have been recorded as well as BAYER the manufacturer who basically says nothing of any consequence. South African case study who did a brief presentation at the European Medical agency. The FDA is also making noises but are they nearly enough?

Summary:
Over 800 million prescriptions for these drugs have been written, but for years patients have been warning of long term devastating side effects. 20 years later the FDA and the European Medical Agency have finally woken up and sounded warnings. Is it enough? What is happening here in South Africa and how was it possible that a group of drugs called Fluoroquinolones that indiscrimininantly destroys mitochondrial DNA, snaps tendons, causes ruptures of the AORTA and provokes psychotic episodes and suicides, is prescribed by doctors around the world without even a warning to their patients. Carte Blanche investigates

Further information:
Its taken 20 years, desperate and damaged patients around the world before the European Union Medicines Agency after hearing testimony released the statement below. As a result the SAHPRA also released a statement - but is that enough for this powerful group of antibiotics that work like chemotherapy and have devastating long term side effects. Carte Blanche tells the story of South Africans who have fought for their lives and fought to be heard when no one believed them.

Disabling and potentially permanent side effects lead to suspension or restrictions of quinolone and fluoroquinolone antibiotics
Press release 16/11/2018
EMA has reviewed serious, disabling and potentially permanent side effects with quinolone and fluoroquinolone antibiotics given by mouth, injection or inhalation. The review incorporated the views of patients, healthcare professionals and academics presented at EMA’s public hearing on fluoroquinolone and quinolone antibiotics in June 2018.
EMA’s human medicines committee (CHMP) has endorsed the recommendations of EMA’s safety committee (PRAC) and concluded that the marketing authorisation of medicines containing cinoxacin, flumequine, nalidixic acid, and pipemidic acid should be suspended.
The CHMP confirmed that the use of the remaining fluoroquinolone antibiotics should be restricted. In addition, the prescribing information for healthcare professionals and information for patients will describe the disabling and potentially permanent side effects and advise patients to stop treatment with a fluoroquinolone antibiotic at the first sign of a side effect involving muscles, tendons or joints and the nervous system.
Restrictions on the use of fluoroquinolone antibiotics will mean that they should not be used:
• to treat infections that might get better without treatment or are not severe (such as throat infections);
• to treat non-bacterial infections, e.g. non-bacterial (chronic) prostatitis;
• for preventing traveller’s diarrhoea or recurring lower urinary tract infections (urine infections that do not extend beyond the bladder);
• to treat mild or moderate bacterial infections unless other antibacterial medicines commonly recommended for these infections cannot be used.
Importantly, fluoroquinolones should generally be avoided in patients who have previously had serious side effects with a fluoroquinolone or quinolone antibiotic. They should be used with special caution in the elderly, patients with kidney disease and those who have had an organ transplantation because these patients are at a higher risk of tendon injury. Since the use of a corticosteroid with a fluoroquinolone also increases this risk, combined use of these medicines should be avoided.
The CHMP opinion will now be forwarded to the European Commission, which will issue a final legally binding decision applicable in all EU countries. National authorities will enforce this decision for the fluoroquinolone and quinolone medicines authorised in their countries and they will also take other appropriate measures to promote the correct use of these antibiotics.
Information for patients
• Fluoroquinolone medicines (which contain ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, lomefloxacin, moxifloxacin, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, pefloxacin, prulifloxacin and rufloxacin) can cause long-lasting, disabling and potentially permanent side effects involving tendons, muscles, joints and the nervous system.
• These serious side effects include inflamed or torn tendon, muscle pain or weakness, and joint pain or swelling, walking difficulty, feeling pins and needles, burning pain, tiredness, depression, problems with memory, sleeping, vision and hearing, and altered taste and smell.
• Tendon swelling and injury may occur within 2 days of starting treatment with a fluoroquinolone but may even occur several months after stopping treatment.
• Stop taking a fluoroquinolone medicine and contact your doctor at once in the following cases:
o at the first sign of tendon injury, such as tendon pain or swelling – rest the painful area;
o if you get pain, feel pins and needles, tingling, tickling, numbness or burning, or weakness especially in the legs or arms;
o if you get swelling in the shoulder, arms or legs, have walking difficulty, feel tired or depressed or have problems with your memory or with sleeping or you notice changes with your vision, taste, smell or hearing. You and your doctor will decide if you can continue treatment or if you need to take another type of antibiotic.
• You may be more prone to joint pain or swelling or tendon damage if you are aged over 60 years, your kidneys do not work well or you have received organ transplantation.
• Speak with your doctor if you are taking a corticosteroid (medicines such as hydrocortisone and prednisolone) or need to have treatment with a corticosteroid. You may be especially prone to tendon damage if you are taking a corticosteroid and a fluoroquinolone medicine at the same time.
• You should not take a fluoroquinolone medicine if you have ever had a serious side effect with a fluoroquinolone or a quinolone medicine and you should speak with your doctor immediately.
• If you have any questions or concerns about your medicines, speak to your doctor or pharmacist.
Information for healthcare professionals
• Fluoroquinolones are associated with prolonged (up to months or years), serious, disabling and potentially irreversible drug reactions affecting several, sometimes multiple, systems, organ classes and senses.
• The serious side effects include tendonitis, tendon rupture, arthralgia, pain in extremities, gait disturbance, neuropathies associated with paraesthesia, depression, fatigue, memory impairment, sleep disorders, and impaired hearing, vision, taste and smell.
• Tendon damage (especially to Achilles tendon but also other tendons) can occur within 48 hours of starting fluoroquinolone treatment but the damage may be delayed several months after stopping treatment.
• Patients who are older, have renal impairment or have had solid organ transplantation and those being treated with a corticosteroid are at higher risk of tendon damage. Concomitant treatment with a fluoroquinolone and a corticosteroid should be avoided.
• Fluoroquinolone treatment should be discontinued at the first sign of tendon pain or inflammation and patients should be advised to stop treatment with a fluoroquinolone and speak with the doctor in case of symptoms of neuropathy such as pain, burning, tingling, numbness or weakness so as to prevent development of potentially irreversible condition.
• Fluoroquinolones should generally not be used in patients who have had serious adverse reactionsassociated with the use of quinolone or fluoroquinolone medicines.
• Up-to-date summary of product characteristics should be consulted for authorised indications when considering treatment with a fluoroquinolone medicine. This is because the indications for these medicines have been restricted.
• The benefits and risks of fluoroquinolones will be monitored continuously and a drug utilisation study will evaluate the effectiveness of the new measures to reduce inappropriate use of fluoroquinolones by investigating changes in prescribing behaviour.

More about the medicine
Fluoroquinolones and quinolones are a class of broad-spectrum antibiotics that are active against bacteria of both Gram-negative and Gram-positive classes. Fluoroquinolones are of value in certain infections, including some life-threatening ones, where alternative antibiotics are not sufficiently effective.
The review covered medicines containing the following fluoroquinolone and quinolone antibiotics: cinoxacin, ciprofloxacin, flumequine, levofloxacin, lomefloxacin, moxifloxacin, nalidixic acid, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, pefloxacin, pipemidic acid, prulifloxacin and rufloxacin.
The review concerned only medicines given systemically (by mouth or injection) and inhaled medicines.
More about the procedure
The review of fluoroquinolones and quinolones was initiated on 9 February 2017 at the request of the German medicines authority (BfArM), under Article 31 of Directive 2001/83/EC.
The review was first carried out by the Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee (PRAC), the Committee responsible for the evaluation of safety issues for human medicines.
The final PRAC recommendations were adopted on 4 October 2018 and then sent to the Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP), responsible for questions concerning medicines for human use, which adopted the Agency’s opinion. The CHMP opinion will now be forwarded to the European Commission, which will issue a final legally binding decision applicable in all EU Member States.

Press Release:


SPECIAL INVESTIGATION: Antibiotic Alert
Around the world millions of prescriptions for fluoroquinolone antibiotics are written every day when this class of drugs should only be a last resort for serious bacterial infections where no other alternative will work. Strenuous warnings from the US Food and Drug Administration, the European Medicines Agency and South African Health Products Regulatory Authority have now been slapped on this drug as reports of devastating side-effects escalate. Consumer activist Erin Brokovich has even lent her name to a patient class action. Carte Blanche investigates the baffling, painful and long-term side-effects of fluoroquinolones.
Producer: Joy Summers
Presenter: Derek Watts
Researcher: Laura Byrne

FINAL SCRIPT ANTIBIOTIC ALERT TX 27th January 2019

Commentary One
Artist and fine art teacher Tracy Witelson, used to run every day, sculpt in wood with chain saws, and live an active life. But on holiday in 2014, she developed a sinus infection and a doctor prescribed her this antibiotic, Ciprobay

Derek
You had only taken three tablets?
Tracy
Yes only three tablets

Commentary Two
Ciprobay belongs to a class of antibiotics called Fluoroquinolones that work differently to other antibiotics. They target the mitochondrial DNA of the bacteria. Only there is a catch, in some people there is an overlap, and it damages their own mitochondrial DNA. Five years, on, Tracy is still battling with the long term side effects

Tracy
The warning I think that is needed, is that the doctors cannot do anything so when it says on the package insert, if you react contact your doctor. The doctor has no treatment, no antidote, no plan! He just goes Oh gee, you are so unlucky, this is very unlucky you are one in a hundred thousand or whatever!

Commentary Three
The compound of Ciprobay is Ciprofloxacin. Bayer, who makes Ciprobay, says that less than 1 % of their patients experience side effects.

TRACY
I came back to Jhb because I was on holiday at the time and saw my GP here and she is an athlete and she said you are in real trouble. Out of however many bad reactions you probably have five and you need to get off your feet, and off work and I was about to open my studio again for the year. I said how long? She said about 2 weeks and you need to get a motorized wheelchair
Derek
As bad as that?
Tracy
Cos, she said these Achilles are going to blow! I landed on that scooter for five months! I could not walk from my bed to the bathroom and that was just the beginning Derek!

LINK
When it was launched in the late 80’s the clinical trials suggested that the drug was relatively safe – the side effects mild and that they were reversible




Commentary Four
Bayer’s patent for Ciprobay expired in 2004 but they still manufacture the drug. I wanted answers, and Bayer’s Medical director Dr Naren Jairam, and head of regulatory affairs Eric Chauke, agreed to meet

Derek
I think Bayer said that there have been over 800 million prescriptions over the years?
Dr Naren Jairam
That’s correct. Ciprobay and Moxifloxacin, the trade name being Avalon has been marketed worldwide in many markets, and the combined use is more than 800 million patients world wide

Commentary Five
And that is just the Bayer Fluoroquinolones. Over 30 companies supply the South African market. We approached eight of them but only Bayer agreed to an on camera interview

Derek
It was a huge money spinner for Bayer, it earned about 2 billion Euros before the patent expired
Dr Naren Jairam
It was an antibiotic that was needed, it was an antibiotic that effectively treated infections, it was an antibiotic that at the time of launch and for many years after that had a favourable benefit risk ratio which has contributed to the sales that it enjoyed

Commentary six
But Tracy Witelson was on the wrong end of that benefit risk ratio and her life came to a standstill. She has been what sufferers now call floxed, a play on the names of the compounds of Fluoroquinolones- like ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and Levofloxacin.

Tracy
After the first month new symptoms appeared, one of them was, the Fluoroquinolones appears to have munched the myelin sheathe, in my nerves from the tips of my toes to my hips and from my fingers all the way across. So it felt as if I had put both my arms and legs in a fire and couldn’t take them out and that lasted five months.
Derek
After being in the wheelchair
Tracy
I was in the fire while I was in the wheelchair

Commentary seven
Tracy also developed a depersonalization disorder which she has reflected in this series of paintings

Tracy
The only evidence I had that I was alive was external, so my…I don’t know what you call it, that fundamental thing that makes you know that you are alive, left. And every thought I had to think, felt like I was swimming over 40 foot wave, just to think it

Commentary eight
But doctors like prescribing these drugs. And they are very effective against life threatening infections like Anthrax, the plague, and multi drug resistant TB. At Groote Schuur we met senior specialist Professor Marc Blockman who is also a pharmacist

Derek
Shouldn’t these drugs be taken off the market?
Marc
These drugs are wonderful in life threatening conditions, they are wonderful agents – MDR TB – rely on one of these agents – to take that away puts the patient at risk of XDRTB
Trivial no, and certainly not first line!

Commentary nine
But that is exactly what doctors were doing, prescribing them like smarties for sinus, ear, bronchial and urinary tract infections. In 2014, Tracy knew nothing of the 2008 FDA black box warning, that Fluoroquinolones are associated with an increased risk of tendinitis and tendon rupture

TRACY
I wasn’t told this is a dangerous antibiotic. Really, it’s like shooting a mosquito with a cannon if you are firing it at a sinus infection.

Commentary ten
Then in 2016, another warning from the FDA. Fluoroquinolones are associated with disabling and potentially permanent serious side effects that can occur together. And importantly that “the risks outweighed the benefits” for simple infections like sinusitis, UTI’s and bronchitis.

Derek
Let’s look at what’s happened from 2016 to2018. FDA warns about disabling side effects, low blood sugar levels, mental health side effects. Mental health? Then ruptures or tears in the aorta blood vessel?
Naren
These safety concerns are not new safety concerns, these were adverse events that were well documented in the literature
Derek
But Naren if these were well documented why weren’t you taking these steps as a pharmaceutical company and warning doctors at least not to prescribe for conditions that were not that serious?
Naren
From a Bayer perspective we always advocated or supported responsible use of antibiotics
Derek
In what way?
Naren
So we always advocated that the Fluoroquinolones should not be used as a first line treatment
Derek
But Naren that is not true.
Naren
What?
Derek
I mean millions of prescriptions are still being made out in America, In Europe in SA, so the message is not getting through, because these aren’t all for life threatening conditions!
Naren
But at the same time you must take into account the millions of patients whose lives have been saved with these antibiotics. So for millions of patients who present with severe infections these antibiotics have saved lives and even changed lives

Commentary eleven
Adcock Ingram also makes these drugs. In a written response to Carte Blanche they say they have received no adverse reports about fluoroquinolones, they support the recent warnings about the drug, and send safety information to healthcare professionals and pharmacists. Fluoroquinolone products, have been successful in treating bacterial infections for many years and new data helps weigh the benefits and risks of the drug.

LINK
There is a common theme running through the stories of those affected – they are shocked by the pain and disability that takes over their lives and after taking the drug they are never the same again

Gerald Ludwinski
How can you be? It changes your DNA, your RNA , you changed a person internally on a cellular level. How can you be the same? You are a mutant!

Commentary twelve
Gerald Ludwinski is a geologist and biochemist. Once a mining engineer, he now works in the wine industry. In 2016, he was prescribed three courses of these antibiotics for an ear infection. With no warning, coupled with doctor ignorance, he was brought to the edge of his pain threshold

Gerald
I said to my wife it’s like someone taking a hacksaw and cutting off my Achilles tendon.

Commentary thirteen
But doctors said his pain was age related. Desperate for help he went to a physician

Gerald
I was crawling to his office, I couldn’t walk anymore I was almost blind, I was almost deaf
Derek
So your hearing and sight was affected?
Gerald
Absolutely! My ear is still affected. I was in so much pain I can’t explain it to people
Derek
One case study says it feels like her legs are on fire
Gerald
Exactly the pain is like a lot of knives stabbing you at the same time and someone putting petrol on you and setting you alight

Commentary fourteen
Gerald had no strength to even pick up the tv remote, and soon ended up in hospital.

Derek
It sounds like you were trying everything just to survive
Gerald
before I went to hospital I crawled to my office and I transferred all my money to my wife account. I thought that was the end of me and I am a very positive person I will fight to the bitter end
Derek
So you were fighting for your life here?
Gerald
Every day since. Every day since

Commentary Fifteen
All three of the antibiotics prescribed to Gerald were made by Cipla. They deferred most of our questions to SAHPRA and say they will abide by their recommendations. They also believe the package insert goes far enough to warn patients of the debilitating and potentially permanent side effects associated with these drugs.

LINK
Around the world patients are claiming that they weren’t adequately warned of the severity of the possible side effects, now you would think that the package insert would make that clear

Derek
I looked up contra indications for CiproBay and it states: “experimental evidence indicates that species variable reversible lesions of weight bearing joints has been seen in immature members of certain animal species” is that right or wrong?
Naren
That is correct, those findings were found and that also guides us in terms of the development of our drugs…
Derek
But is your intention to obfuscate or clarify?
Naren
No I think the intention is to inform the medical community that these adverse events can occur
Derek
But what am I meant to take from that Naren! Couldn’t you just say: look you could snap your Achilles tendon if you take this drug?!


Naren
Look I think our prescribing information that you are referring to is information that has been approved by regulatory authorities
Derek
Is that an excuse?
Naren.
No its not! We comply with the requirements of our regulatory authorities

LINK
By 2018 the revelations of the floxed network could no longer be ignored and Germany asked the European Medicines Agency to review the side effects of these antibiotics

Commentary sixteen
That took place in London last year, where the safety committee of the European medicines agency heard the stories of doctors, pharmacists and support groups representing thousands of people damaged by Fluoroquinolones. Bayer apologized, but defended their drug.

Bayer
I want to express to those of you who expressed your stories today how deeply sorry I am for the experiences you had

Commentary seventeen
Also at the hearing was South African Debbi Kinrade, patient turned activist who now lives in the UK. She first took the antibiotics in 2012 and told me her story before she flew back home.

Debbi, briefly go through your story?

Debbi
The first part was tendons mainly Achilles- moved to my shoulders very briskly, I found it difficult to breathe and move and then severe headaches- intense pain I was unable to eat, and then started to cross brain barrier, so my cognitive function poor, very blurred vision, my concentration was bad, lost sense of taste. insomnia, inability to cope with stress. I found it difficult to drive …lost my confidence- happening so rapidly …. makes me emotional Because it was happening so rapidly and I was so bewildered, I didn’t tell anybody. I felt ashamed that my brain was letting me down, so I hid it as much as I could even from husband

Commentary eighteen
Debbi says she wouldn’t have survived without the support of her husband and family. but after two years with little change in her condition, she made a radical decision.

Debbi
I had decided that if I didn’t find a way forward in the next couple of months that I would actually commit suicide, because I could not live with the way my life had become so small and so scary and I had such a fear for the future.

Commentary nineteen
Sheer determination, 7 years and thousands spent on treatment, has helped her retrieve 90% of her functioning. She has also dedicated much of her time to research and helping others through support groups.

Derek
What was the common thread going through the support groups?
Debbi
That people had not gotten a diagnosis, that they were ridiculed and laughed at told that it was in their imagination even though couldn’t walk, and they were very desperate for some kind of understanding and so they come to the groups looking for support really.

Commentary twenty
The drug companies insist the side effects are rare, but the floxed network say a million adverse events have been reported in America alone, and they claim the real numbers are much higher

Debbi
Ya they keep talking about rare but we hear figures from Bayer that its one percent well on 800 million that’s 8 million people. Its increasingly obvious from the amount of investigation that governments have done it’s not rare otherwise they wouldn’t take the kind of steps they are taking to mitigate against the drugs

Commentary twenty one
But if Bayer and the other Big Pharma companies knew about the severity of the side effects, were they adequately warning the doctors? Bayer’s head of regulatory affairs Erik Chauke says they were

Derek
Now Naren says there is proof that you have advised practitioners only to prescribe the drug where there is no alternative, have you got that proof
Eric
Yes, we have some of those information, so this is a very general one and this is to patients, but it doesn’t have products
Derek
Eric there is a huge difference between this ABC of antibiotics and these dire warnings from the FDA.
Eric
That is just one of the communications we would send out there
Derek
I am not seeing a warning Eric; can you show me something that says this can have dreadful side effects and leave you virtually crippled
Eric
As you can see there, this is what we communicate to doctors- musculoskeletal complications of Fluoroquinolones.



Commentary twenty two
Two months ago the European medicines agency said they would be recommending restrictions on the use of these antibiotics.

Derek
Here the EMA talks about disabling and potentially permanent side effects
Dr Naren
Well a lot of the evidence suggests its prolonged as opposed to permanent
Derek
Well it ends when you die, I guess?
Naren
No, it can vary from patient to patient
Derek
Ya but either way potentially permanent or prolonged it’s not good is it?
Naren
You know once again these adverse events you are referring to are known and we express deep sadness to patients who experience these events, but the benefit still outweighs the risk
Derek
So sorry for you if you are part of those hundreds of thousands who did get the side effects Naren
Once again, its importance… as well that these antibiotics are used appropriately and responsibly to minimize the adverse events that can occur in patients

Commentary twenty three
As chair of the pharmacovigilance committee of our own regulatory body SAHPRA, Professor Blockman co- authored the local warning, following the European medicines agency recommendations

Derek
Is SAHPRA doing enough?
Professor Marc Blockman
I think they are. Often it takes a while because you have to collaborate with the companies and often there will be arm wrestling to decide
Derek
Some say the SAHPRA warning is tame even in comparison to the FDA?
Prof Marc Blockman
If you look at the heading, the heading is very clear in terms of disabling and potentially long lasting. If all that you read that a really telling head that is not pulling the punches.
Derek
You know maybe I am being simplistic, but can’t we just send out a message to doctors tomorrow -don’t prescribe these conditions unless they are life threatening and there is no alternative simple as that?
Professor Marc Blockman
So I think the international regulatory authorities are making that recommendation to try and change practice behavior

Derek
Where to now?
Professor Marc Blockman
This conversation is very important. I am hoping that patients take note, that doctors take extra note, and what we will be doing is asking the companies themselves how are you going to get medical practitioners to come in line. You need to take some responsibility for the prescribing of your medicine as well

Commentary twenty four
But those affected are on their own. Gerald’s recovery started with only 20 steps. He has lost 38 kilograms and much of his muscle mass. He uses exercise to keep depression at bay, as he tries to rebuild his broken body. Despite the pain he walks several hours daily

Gerald
I haven’t given up. I am trying basically even things I don’t believe in, because I have tried every pain medicine on the market and even those that aren’t on the market- I have tried.

Tracy
I cant run I cant sculpt I cant jump. I have problems with my memory I am in chronic pain.
Derek
You must get angry at times?
Tracy
Ya I am furious! And I keep hearing new stories and I keep meeting people who have had these experiences

Disabling and potentially permanent side effects lead to suspension or restrictions of quinolone and fluoroquinolone antibiotics Press release 16/11/2018 EMA has reviewed serious, disabling and potentially permanent side effects with quinolone and fluoroquinolone antibiotics given by mouth, injection or inhalation. The review incorporated the views of patients, healthcare professionals and academics presented at EMA’s public hearing on fluoroquinolone and quinolone antibiotics in June 2018. EMA’s human medicines committee (CHMP) has endorsed the recommendations of EMA’s safety committee (PRAC) and concluded that the marketing authorisation of medicines containing cinoxacin, flumequine, nalidixic acid, and pipemidic acid should be suspended. The CHMP confirmed that the use of the remaining fluoroquinolone antibiotics should be restricted. In addition, the prescribing information for healthcare professionals and information for patients will describe the disabling and potentially permanent side effects and advise patients to stop treatment with a fluoroquinolone antibiotic at the first sign of a side effect involving muscles, tendons or joints and the nervous system. Restrictions on the use of fluoroquinolone antibiotics will mean that they should not be used: • to treat infections that might get better without treatment or are not severe (such as throat infections); • to treat non-bacterial infections, e.g. non-bacterial (chronic) prostatitis; • for preventing traveller’s diarrhoea or recurring lower urinary tract infections (urine infections that do not extend beyond the bladder); • to treat mild or moderate bacterial infections unless other antibacterial medicines commonly recommended for these infections cannot be used. Importantly, fluoroquinolones should generally be avoided in patients who have previously had serious side effects with a fluoroquinolone or quinolone antibiotic. They should be used with special caution in the elderly, patients with kidney disease and those who have had an organ transplantation because these patients are at a higher risk of tendon injury. Since the use of a corticosteroid with a fluoroquinolone also increases this risk, combined use of these medicines should be avoided. The CHMP opinion will now be forwarded to the European Commission, which will issue a final legally binding decision applicable in all EU countries. National authorities will enforce this decision for the fluoroquinolone and quinolone medicines authorised in their countries and they will also take other appropriate measures to promote the correct use of these antibiotics. Information for patients • Fluoroquinolone medicines (which contain ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, lomefloxacin, moxifloxacin, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, pefloxacin, prulifloxacin and rufloxacin) can cause long-lasting, disabling and potentially permanent side effects involving tendons, muscles, joints and the nervous system. • These serious side effects include inflamed or torn tendon, muscle pain or weakness, and joint pain or swelling, walking difficulty, feeling pins and needles, burning pain, tiredness, depression, problems with memory, sleeping, vision and hearing, and altered taste and smell. • Tendon swelling and injury may occur within 2 days of starting treatment with a fluoroquinolone but may even occur several months after stopping treatment. • Stop taking a fluoroquinolone medicine and contact your doctor at once in the following cases: o at the first sign of tendon injury, such as tendon pain or swelling – rest the painful area; o if you get pain, feel pins and needles, tingling, tickling, numbness or burning, or weakness especially in the legs or arms; o if you get swelling in the shoulder, arms or legs, have walking difficulty, feel tired or depressed or have problems with your memory or with sleeping or you notice changes with your vision, taste, smell or hearing. You and your doctor will decide if you can continue treatment or if you need to take another type of antibiotic. • You may be more prone to joint pain or swelling or tendon damage if you are aged over 60 years, your kidneys do not work well or you have received organ transplantation. • Speak with your doctor if you are taking a corticosteroid (medicines such as hydrocortisone and prednisolone) or need to have treatment with a corticosteroid. You may be especially prone to tendon damage if you are taking a corticosteroid and a fluoroquinolone medicine at the same time. • You should not take a fluoroquinolone medicine if you have ever had a serious side effect with a fluoroquinolone or a quinolone medicine and you should speak with your doctor immediately. • If you have any questions or concerns about your medicines, speak to your doctor or pharmacist. Information for healthcare professionals • Fluoroquinolones are associated with prolonged (up to months or years), serious, disabling and potentially irreversible drug reactions affecting several, sometimes multiple, systems, organ classes and senses. • The serious side effects include tendonitis, tendon rupture, arthralgia, pain in extremities, gait disturbance, neuropathies associated with paraesthesia, depression, fatigue, memory impairment, sleep disorders, and impaired hearing, vision, taste and smell. • Tendon damage (especially to Achilles tendon but also other tendons) can occur within 48 hours of starting fluoroquinolone treatment but the damage may be delayed several months after stopping treatment. • Patients who are older, have renal impairment or have had solid organ transplantation and those being treated with a corticosteroid are at higher risk of tendon damage. Concomitant treatment with a fluoroquinolone and a corticosteroid should be avoided. • Fluoroquinolone treatment should be discontinued at the first sign of tendon pain or inflammation and patients should be advised to stop treatment with a fluoroquinolone and speak with the doctor in case of symptoms of neuropathy such as pain, burning, tingling, numbness or weakness so as to prevent development of potentially irreversible condition. • Fluoroquinolones should generally not be used in patients who have had serious adverse reactionsassociated with the use of quinolone or fluoroquinolone medicines. • Up-to-date summary of product characteristics should be consulted for authorised indications when considering treatment with a fluoroquinolone medicine. This is because the indications for these medicines have been restricted. • The benefits and risks of fluoroquinolones will be monitored continuously and a drug utilisation study will evaluate the effectiveness of the new measures to reduce inappropriate use of fluoroquinolones by investigating changes in prescribing behaviour. More about the medicine Fluoroquinolones and quinolones are a class of broad-spectrum antibiotics that are active against bacteria of both Gram-negative and Gram-positive classes. Fluoroquinolones are of value in certain infections, including some life-threatening ones, where alternative antibiotics are not sufficiently effective. The review covered medicines containing the following fluoroquinolone and quinolone antibiotics: cinoxacin, ciprofloxacin, flumequine, levofloxacin, lomefloxacin, moxifloxacin, nalidixic acid, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, pefloxacin, pipemidic acid, prulifloxacin and rufloxacin. The review concerned only medicines given systemically (by mouth or injection) and inhaled medicines. More about the procedure The review of fluoroquinolones and quinolones was initiated on 9 February 2017 at the request of the German medicines authority (BfArM), under Article 31 of Directive 2001/83/EC. The review was first carried out by the Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee (PRAC), the Committee responsible for the evaluation of safety issues for human medicines. The final PRAC recommendations were adopted on 4 October 2018 and then sent to the Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP), responsible for questions concerning medicines for human use, which adopted the Agency’s opinion. The CHMP opinion will now be forwarded to the European Commission, which will issue a final legally binding decision applicable in all EU Member States. metadata.Summary: Over 800 million prescriptions for these drugs have been written, but for years patients have been warning of long term devastating side effects. 20 years later the FDA and the European Medical Agency have finally woken up and sounded warnings. Is it enough? metadata.Further information: Its taken 20 years, desperate and damaged patients around the world before the European Union Medicines Agency after hearing testimony released the statement below. As a result the SAHPRA also released a statement - but is that enough for this powerful group of antibiotics that work like chemotherapy and have devastating long term side effects. Carte Blanche tells the story of South Africans who have fought for their lives and fought to be heard when no one believed them. Disabling and potentially permanent side effects lead to suspension or restrictions of quinolone and fluoroquinolone antibiotics Press release 16/11/2018 EMA has reviewed serious, disabling and potentially permanent side effects with quinolone and fluoroquinolone antibiotics given by mouth, injection or inhalation. The review incorporated the views of patients, healthcare professionals and academics presented at EMA’s public hearing on fluoroquinolone and quinolone antibiotics in June 2018. EMA’s human medicines committee (CHMP) has endorsed the recommendations of EMA’s safety committee (PRAC) and concluded that the marketing authorisation of medicines containing cinoxacin, flumequine, nalidixic acid, and pipemidic acid should be suspended. The CHMP confirmed that the use of the remaining fluoroquinolone antibiotics should be restricted. In addition, the prescribing information for healthcare professionals and information for patients will describe the disabling and potentially permanent side effects and advise patients to stop treatment with a fluoroquinolone antibiotic at the first sign of a side effect involving muscles, tendons or joints and the nervous system. Restrictions on the use of fluoroquinolone antibiotics will mean that they should not be used: • to treat infections that might get better without treatment or are not severe (such as throat infections); • to treat non-bacterial infections, e.g. non-bacterial (chronic) prostatitis; • for preventing traveller’s diarrhoea or recurring lower urinary tract infections (urine infections that do not extend beyond the bladder); • to treat mild or moderate bacterial infections unless other antibacterial medicines commonly recommended for these infections cannot be used. Importantly, fluoroquinolones should generally be avoided in patients who have previously had serious side effects with a fluoroquinolone or quinolone antibiotic. They should be used with special caution in the elderly, patients with kidney disease and those who have had an organ transplantation because these patients are at a higher risk of tendon injury. Since the use of a corticosteroid with a fluoroquinolone also increases this risk, combined use of these medicines should be avoided. The CHMP opinion will now be forwarded to the European Commission, which will issue a final legally binding decision applicable in all EU countries. National authorities will enforce this decision for the fluoroquinolone and quinolone medicines authorised in their countries and they will also take other appropriate measures to promote the correct use of these antibiotics. Information for patients • Fluoroquinolone medicines (which contain ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, lomefloxacin, moxifloxacin, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, pefloxacin, prulifloxacin and rufloxacin) can cause long-lasting, disabling and potentially permanent side effects involving tendons, muscles, joints and the nervous system. • These serious side effects include inflamed or torn tendon, muscle pain or weakness, and joint pain or swelling, walking difficulty, feeling pins and needles, burning pain, tiredness, depression, problems with memory, sleeping, vision and hearing, and altered taste and smell. • Tendon swelling and injury may occur within 2 days of starting treatment with a fluoroquinolone but may even occur several months after stopping treatment. • Stop taking a fluoroquinolone medicine and contact your doctor at once in the following cases: o at the first sign of tendon injury, such as tendon pain or swelling – rest the painful area; o if you get pain, feel pins and needles, tingling, tickling, numbness or burning, or weakness especially in the legs or arms; o if you get swelling in the shoulder, arms or legs, have walking difficulty, feel tired or depressed or have problems with your memory or with sleeping or you notice changes with your vision, taste, smell or hearing. You and your doctor will decide if you can continue treatment or if you need to take another type of antibiotic. • You may be more prone to joint pain or swelling or tendon damage if you are aged over 60 years, your kidneys do not work well or you have received organ transplantation. • Speak with your doctor if you are taking a corticosteroid (medicines such as hydrocortisone and prednisolone) or need to have treatment with a corticosteroid. You may be especially prone to tendon damage if you are taking a corticosteroid and a fluoroquinolone medicine at the same time. • You should not take a fluoroquinolone medicine if you have ever had a serious side effect with a fluoroquinolone or a quinolone medicine and you should speak with your doctor immediately. • If you have any questions or concerns about your medicines, speak to your doctor or pharmacist. Information for healthcare professionals • Fluoroquinolones are associated with prolonged (up to months or years), serious, disabling and potentially irreversible drug reactions affecting several, sometimes multiple, systems, organ classes and senses. • The serious side effects include tendonitis, tendon rupture, arthralgia, pain in extremities, gait disturbance, neuropathies associated with paraesthesia, depression, fatigue, memory impairment, sleep disorders, and impaired hearing, vision, taste and smell. • Tendon damage (especially to Achilles tendon but also other tendons) can occur within 48 hours of starting fluoroquinolone treatment but the damage may be delayed several months after stopping treatment. • Patients who are older, have renal impairment or have had solid organ transplantation and those being treated with a corticosteroid are at higher risk of tendon damage. Concomitant treatment with a fluoroquinolone and a corticosteroid should be avoided. • Fluoroquinolone treatment should be discontinued at the first sign of tendon pain or inflammation and patients should be advised to stop treatment with a fluoroquinolone and speak with the doctor in case of symptoms of neuropathy such as pain, burning, tingling, numbness or weakness so as to prevent development of potentially irreversible condition. • Fluoroquinolones should generally not be used in patients who have had serious adverse reactionsassociated with the use of quinolone or fluoroquinolone medicines. • Up-to-date summary of product characteristics should be consulted for authorised indications when considering treatment with a fluoroquinolone medicine. This is because the indications for these medicines have been restricted. • The benefits and risks of fluoroquinolones will be monitored continuously and a drug utilisation study will evaluate the effectiveness of the new measures to reduce inappropriate use of fluoroquinolones by investigating changes in prescribing behaviour. More about the medicine Fluoroquinolones and quinolones are a class of broad-spectrum antibiotics that are active against bacteria of both Gram-negative and Gram-positive classes. Fluoroquinolones are of value in certain infections, including some life-threatening ones, where alternative antibiotics are not sufficiently effective. The review covered medicines containing the following fluoroquinolone and quinolone antibiotics: cinoxacin, ciprofloxacin, flumequine, levofloxacin, lomefloxacin, moxifloxacin, nalidixic acid, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, pefloxacin, pipemidic acid, prulifloxacin and rufloxacin. The review concerned only medicines given systemically (by mouth or injection) and inhaled medicines. More about the procedure The review of fluoroquinolones and quinolones was initiated on 9 February 2017 at the request of the German medicines authority (BfArM), under Article 31 of Directive 2001/83/EC. The review was first carried out by the Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee (PRAC), the Committee responsible for the evaluation of safety issues for human medicines. The final PRAC recommendations were adopted on 4 October 2018 and then sent to the Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP), responsible for questions concerning medicines for human use, which adopted the Agency’s opinion. The CHMP opinion will now be forwarded to the European Commission, which will issue a final legally binding decision applicable in all EU Member States.
